messages.body_plain:

I am using spec() on acceleration data (unit: m/s2).

code:

spec(wave=data, wn ="hanning", f=sampfreq, norm=F, wl=windowlen, plot=F)

My question is, given the output of this function call, are the units of "amplitude" (y-axis) the same as in the original data passed to the "wave" parameter (i.e m/s2)?

Thanks

messages.subject: spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.subject_clean: spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a small question regarding the spec() function after reading the code (seewave 1.7.3). It appears that even when we supply 'from' and 'to' arguments, the x-axis is scaled as:

> x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/wl), length.out = n%/%2)/1000

using the default window length of wl = 512 rather than, say wl = b - a. I suspect this might possibly lead to a slightly imperfect scaling. One can also supply their own wl arguments (say, wl = 2) and get clearly incorrectly scaled spectral slices.

I am also a bit unclear on the need for the (f/wl) term in the first place. Is it correcting for something in particular that I'm missing?

Thanks,
-Arvind

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.body_plain:
Dear Arvind,

The arguments 'from' and 'to' refer to the time scale.
For instance the compute the spectrum of the first note of tico, you
should run:

data(tico)
spec(tico, from=0, to=0.5)

Now if you wish to zoom along the frequency x-axis you should use the
argument 'flim'. For instance, to zoom in between 2 and 6 kHz for the
first note:

spec(tico, from=0, to=0.5, flim=c(2,6))

Best regards,

Jerome

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] spec() frequency axis scaling with 'from' and 'to' args
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jérôme,
Thanks for the prompt response.

I understand that 'from' and 'to' are used to specify a time slice of the original wave object, just as 'at=0.5' and 'wl=512' refer to a time-slice corresponding to a window of length 512 points around the specified time-point.

I assumed that the window-length argument doesn't have a meaning when the user explicitly specifies the lower and upper time bounds of the window (or at least wl should be computed rather than being specified as an argument). Yet the default value of the wl argument is still being used to compute the x-axis later on, even if it doesn't correspond to the true window length of the time slice taken.

I think the following line addition should do the right thing:

    if (!is.null(from) | !is.null(to)) {
        if (is.null(from) && !is.null(to)) {
            a <- 1
            b <- round(to * f)
        ...

            else a <- round(from * f)
            b <- round(to * f)
        }
        wl <- b - a  # set the correct window length
        wave <- as.matrix(wave[a:b, ])
    }

Thanks,
-Arvind

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Just got an idea from a colleague that is going to solve the problem:

Hi,

I think you are almost there. The problem is that the recorder is adding some metadata that is not based on the standard, so this has to be customized.

Just add a substring extraction if the position stays the same. The first number is where it starts and the second number is how many letters to use:

======
$ filehead=$(head -c 1024 STE-077.wav)
$ echo ${filehead:40:10}

2013-08-15

$ echo ${filehead:50:8}

09:38:52
======

You should be able to run this from R using the function system().

messages.subject: spec() function x-axis calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I was wondering if someone could explain why the x-axis calculation for the spectrum in the spec() function:

    x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/wl), length.out = n%/%2)/1000

includes the f/wl term.  I saw from Arvind Sowmyan's previous thread that there was a small bug with the definition of wl when from and to are specified.  But I'm still not quite sure why there is this f/wl term.  If there were just the f/2 term, that makes sense to me because that would be the Nyquist frequency.  How does the f/wl term come in?  I apologize for the naive question---I'm pretty inexperienced with DSP.

Thank you very much,
Kristine

Dear Kristine,

f/2 is the Nyquist frequency.
f/wl is the frequency resolution of the FFT or the bin width of the FFT. If you have a 44100 Hz sampling frequency and that you set up the length of the FFT window (wl) at 512 samples, the spectrum will have a frequency resolution of f/wl = 86.13 Hz. A spectrum is usually drawn with lines as it was continuous but it should actually plotted as a barplot.
The x-axis of the spec() and meanspec() ends at the Nyquist frequency - 1 spectrum bin, this is to avoid the Nyquist frequency, just be one step below.
HTH
Jerome

messages.subject: Preventing memory problems with savewav and large audio files
messages.subject_clean: Preventing memory problems with savewav and large audio files
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using tuneR and seewave to read in .MP3 files, extract the left channel, and save it, roughly like this:

> library(tuneR); library(seewave)

> z <- mono(readMP3("MP3_file.MP3"), "left")                   # read MP3 and take only left channel
>
> savewav(z, filename = paste0("left", "MP3_file.MP3"))     # save the left channel into a new final
> rm(z)                                                                          # remove the object, move to next file

This works great when my input .MP3 (44.1 kHz, stereo, 16-bit) files are less than about 45 MB.  But on my 8 GB 64-bit Windows machine without any other programs open, going much beyond this causes either errors or warnings regarding memory limits (see below) during the the call to savewav.  Is there some better way to go about this task that would prevent errors and warnings?  I looked into some of the packages in the Cran Task View for high-performance computing, but it wasn't immediately apparent to me that any of them could help with audio files.  Will it be necessary to move out of R or to cut these files into smaller pieces and somehow join the smaller saved files together afterwards?  Any advice would be appreciated.

Here is an example error:

> Error in validObject(.Object) :
>   invalid class “WaveMC” object: Error : cannot allocate vector of size 1.3 Gb
> In addition: Warning messages:
> 1: In structure(list(message = as.character(message), call = call),  :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)
> 2: In structure(list(message = as.character(message), call = call),  :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)
> 3: In structure(list(message = as.character(message), call = call),  :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)
> 4: In structure(list(message = as.character(message), call = call),  :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)

and here is an example warning from trying this process on a 52 MB file

> Warning messages:
> 1: In writeWave(wave, filename = filename) :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)
> 2: In writeWave(wave, filename = filename) :
>   Reached total allocation of 8081Mb: see help(memory.size)
